sudan.content: يونيسف: 67% من الأسر في السودان تعاني انعدام الأمن المائي تخطّي إلى المحتوى صحيفة عاجل الإلكترونية النشرة البريدية اتصل بنا تابعنا: ابحث في عاجل… اللغات الرئيسية المحليات الاقتصاد رياضة مدارات عالمية وظائف الترفيه منوعات سياحة وسفر مجتمع كل الأقسام الرئيسية ‹ مدارات عالمية ‹ الخبر مدارات عالمية دقيقة قراءة يونيسف: 67% من أسر السودان تعاني انعدام الأمن المائي فريق التحرير نُشر في الأربعاء 21 أكتوبر 2026 · 2:23 م ملخّص إيجاز بالذكاء الاصطناعي النشرة البريدية أهم الأخبار إلى بريدك كل صباح. بريدك الإلكتروني اشترك الآن اسأل الخبر مساعد ذكي يجيب من سياق الخبر فقط اسأل ما تريد عن هذا الخبر ما الفكرة الرئيسية للخبر؟ ما هي أبرز الأرقام والإحصاءات؟ كيف يؤثر هذا علي؟ صحيفة إلكترونية سعودية تم تأسيسها عام 2007م تهتم بنشر الأخبار المحلية والمنافسة في سبق الأخبار بمهنية ومصداقية وموضوعية ★ اجعل «عاجل» مصدرك المفضل في قوقل الأقسام المحليات الاقتصاد رياضة مدارات عالمية وظائف الترفيه روابط سريعة الرئيسية مقالات الرأي البحث النشرة البريدية الصحيفة من نحن اتصل بنا أعلن معنا سياسة الخصوصية جميع الحقوق محفوظة لـ شركة إيجاز للنشر الإلكتروني المالكة لصحيفة عاجل شروط الاستخدام أعلنت منظمة الأمم المتحدة للطفولة (يونيسف) ومجموعة المياه والصرف الصحي والنظافة التابعة للأمم المتحدة أن 67% من الأسر في السودان تعاني انعدام الأمن المائي. وذكرت المنظمتان في تقرير استند إلى نتائج التقييم متعدد القطاعات للاحتياجات، الذي أُجري في يوليو 2026، أن 41.2% من الأسر تفتقر إلى خدمات المياه الأساسية، بينما تفتقر 53.7% إلى الحد الأدنى من خدمات الصرف الصحي، و46.8% إلى خدمات النظافة الأساسية. وأوضح التقرير أن المسح شمل 23,736 أسرة في جميع ولايات السودان، ورصد مستويات الخدمات المتوفرة ومظاهر انعدام الأمن المائي وأساليب التكيف التي تعتمدها الأسر لمواجهة نقص المياه، إضافة إلى العوائق التي تحول دون تلبية احتياجاتها من المياه والصرف الصحي. ناقش الخبر مع الذكاء الاصطناعي ChatGPT Gemini Claude Grok التعليقات ( 0 ) نشر التعليق

رفضاً لإخلاء داخلية أبو دجانة أمستردام: الخرطوم: كمبالا / الأربعاء 21 أكتوبر 2026 توافد طلاب من كلية الهندسة وكليات أخرى بجامعة الخرطوم إلى داخلية أبو دجانة، تضامناً مع زملائهم المقيمين فيها، واحتجاجاً على قرار إدارة الجامعة والصندوق القومي لرعاية الطلاب بإخلاء المبنى ونقلهم إلى مجمع كلية التربية بأم درمان، لإفساح المجال أمام إسكان الطالبات بصورة مؤقتة. و ظلت داخلية أبو دجانة تاريخياً مخصصة بصورة أساسية لطلاب الهندسة في المستويات الثالث والرابع والخامس، واقتصر السكن فيها خلال بعض السنوات على طلاب المستويين الرابع والخامس. ومع اقتراب موعد استئناف الدراسة بالكلية في 24 أكتوبر الجاري، يواجه طلاب الداخلية، أعباء إضافية تتمثل في الانتقال إلى مجمع كلية التربية بأم درمان، والتنقل يومياً إلى كليتهم بالخرطوم، بتكلفة مواصلات قد تصل إلى نحو 14 ألف جنيه سوداني للطالب يومياً، وفقاً لمنصة جامعة الخرطوم، في ظل عدم توفير الإدارة، وسيلة ترحيل منتظمة بين المجمعين. وأوضح مصدر مطلع بالجامعة أن الداخلية شهدت خلال الفترة الماضية أعمال صيانة وتأهيل بمبادرات من الجمعية الهندسية التسييرية، وبمساهمات من مهندسين وخريجين، ورجح أن تكون جاهزية أبو دجانة أحد الأسباب التي دفعت الجهات المعنية إلى اختيارها لإسكان الطالبات مؤقتاً. رفض للقرار وبحسب بيان صادر عن لجنة طلاب داخلية أبو دجانة، اطلعت عليه (دبنقا)، رفض الطلاب القرار وتمسكوا بالبقاء في غرفهم، مشككين في إمكانية العودة خلال الفترة المحددة التي تتراوح بين 15 و20 يوماً، مستندين إلى تجارب سابقة لإخلاء داخليات البركس والوسط، إلى جانب داخلية عبد السلام بشمبات، التي قالوا إن طلابها أُخرجوا منها دون توفير بديل. من جانبها أعلنت الجمعية الهندسية التسييرية بكلية الهندسة رفضها الكامل لقرار الإخلاء، ودعت طلاب الكلية إلى البقاء في الداخلية وعدم الاستجابة لطلبات المغادرة، معتبرة أن الخطوة تعكس عدم اكتمال استعدادات الجامعة لاستقبال الطلاب والطالبات. ودعت اللجنة الطلاب إلى مواصلة التواجد في الداخلية، محذرة من احتمال محاولة تنفيذ قرار الإخلاء بالقوة، في وقت لا تزال فيه الأزمة دون حسم، وسط مطالبات لإدارة الجامعة والصندوق القومي لرعاية الطلاب بإيجاد حلول تضمن حقوق جميع الطلاب والطالبات. Published 12 minutes ago on October 21, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki meet in Eritrea on March 3, 2019. File photo. Credit: Office of the Prime Minister of Ethiopia Diplomatic tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea remain unresolved despite international appeals for restraint, with the neighboring countries continuing to exchange accusations over territorial security, armed opposition groups and access to the Red Sea. The confrontation has intensified following Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s October 19 warning that Eritrea could face severe consequences if it continued providing support to groups opposing his government. In a Tigrigna-language interview broadcast by Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC), Abiy accused Eritrea of allowing its territory to serve as a base for forces hostile to Ethiopia while maintaining that peaceful cooperation remained possible. The remarks, detailed in Kulu Media’s report on Abiy’s warning , came amid renewed military operations in Tigray and heightened concern over the possibility of a wider regional confrontation. Eritrea has rejected Ethiopian accusations of supporting armed opposition groups. Asmara has instead accused Addis Ababa of threatening its sovereignty through demands for greater access to the Red Sea. International Pressure for De-escalation The United States and United Kingdom have urged both governments to avoid further escalation and resolve their differences through diplomacy. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called for restraint during discussions with Abiy Ahmed, emphasizing respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity. The United Kingdom subsequently urged renewed diplomatic engagement and expressed support for African Union efforts to reduce tensions. As detailed in Kulu Media’s coverage of the UK’s diplomatic appeal , London also warned about the humanitarian consequences of renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia. The Associated Press reported that international concerns have increased as renewed fighting in Tigray places additional pressure on the fragile security arrangements established after the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement. Competing Claims Over Border Security Ethiopia has accused Eritrean forces of entering its territory and supporting insurgent groups, allegations Eritrea disputes. Earlier this month, Ethiopia informed the United Nations Security Council that it was invoking its right to self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter. Eritrea rejected that justification and accused Ethiopia of threatening its territorial integrity. The Associated Press reported that the competing allegations could not be independently verified in full. The confrontation has also been complicated by Ethiopia’s longstanding interest in securing reliable maritime access, including through arrangements involving Red Sea ports. Eritrea regards any attempt to obtain sovereign control over its territory as a threat to national sovereignty. Despite repeated international calls for dialogue, there has been no independently confirmed agreement on a new ceasefire, military withdrawal or formal bilateral negotiation process. The absence of such an agreement leaves the relationship vulnerable to further deterioration as military and political developments continue in northern Ethiopia. Image Credit: EBC / Screenshot by Kulu Media Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has warned Eritrea of severe consequences if it continues to support armed groups opposing his government, delivering one of his clearest public warnings to the neighboring country amid renewed fighting in Tigray and growing fears of a wider regional conflict. Speaking in a Tigrigna-language interview broadcast by the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC) on Monday, October 19, Abiy accused Eritrea of allowing its territory to be used by groups hostile to Ethiopia. The prime minister said cooperation between the two countries would offer greater benefits than confrontation and warned against ignoring Ethiopia’s appeals. According to Interview , Abiy said Eritrea’s continued role as a base for Ethiopia’s adversaries would bring severe consequences. The warning marks a further escalation in rhetoric between Addis Ababa and Asmara, which severed diplomatic relations earlier this month following competing allegations of military aggression and interference in each other’s internal affairs. Ethiopia has repeatedly accused Eritrea of supporting the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and other armed opposition groups. Eritrea has rejected accusations that it is backing Ethiopian rebels and has accused Addis Ababa of pursuing hostile policies toward its sovereignty. Warning Comes Amid Renewed Tigray Conflict Abiy’s remarks followed weeks of military operations in Tigray, where Ethiopian federal forces and allied Tigray Peace Force (TPF) fighters have regained control of several major towns previously held by TPLF-aligned forces. The military developments have brought Ethiopian government forces closer to Eritrea’s border, intensifying concerns that the confrontation could expand beyond Tigray. As documented in Kulu Media’s coverage of the border tensions , troop movements, disputed territorial claims and the collapse of diplomatic relations have increased the risk of direct confrontation between the two countries. Earlier in October, Ethiopia accused Eritrean troops of crossing into its territory and occupying parts of northern Tigray. The Ethiopian government subsequently invoked Article 51 of the United Nations Charter, asserting its right to self-defense. Eritrea, meanwhile, called for UN action against Ethiopia, accusing Addis Ababa of preparing military aggression. The competing accusations have not been independently established in full. Abiy Says TPLF Is Nearing Its End During the interview, Abiy also addressed the TPLF’s declining control over major towns in Tigray following the latest federal military offensive. He suggested that the organization was approaching the end of its political dominance and pledged development across the region. His comments came days after the federal government established a caretaker administration with a six-month mandate to restore public services, improve security and prepare for regional elections. The TPLF-aligned leadership has rejected the new administration, challenging its legitimacy and the authority of its decisions. Abiy urged Tigray residents to preserve unity and public institutions while preparations for a future elected administration continue. Despite the federal government’s territorial gains, the security situation remains uncertain in some parts of Tigray, and political disagreements over the region’s future remain unresolved. Ethiopia and Eritrea Remain on Opposing Diplomatic Paths Relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea have deteriorated sharply since the two countries restored diplomatic ties in 2018. The former allies fought together against the TPLF during the 2020–2022 Tigray war, but their relationship subsequently worsened over regional security, the Pretoria peace agreement and Ethiopia’s ambitions for greater access to the Red Sea. Abiy’s latest remarks combined a warning against alleged Eritrean interference with an appeal for peaceful cooperation. He said good neighborly relations and partnership remained the appropriate path forward. International concern has also increased. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently warned of wider war and urged restraint as military tensions continued along the border. Abiy’s October 19 warning does not amount to a formal declaration of war or an announcement of a new military offensive against Eritrea. However, the direct warning from Ethiopia’s prime minister adds another layer of political tension to an already volatile confrontation, with renewed fighting in Tigray threatening to destabilize the wider Horn of Africa. Published 3 days ago on October 18, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on October 18, 2026, that US intelligence sharing had resumed following a temporary interruption. File Photo. Credit: Press Service of the President of Ukraine, via Wikimedia Commons The United States has resumed intelligence sharing with Ukraine after a three-day interruption that affected warnings about incoming Russian ballistic missiles, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday, confirming the restoration of a critical part of Washington’s military assistance to Kyiv. In an interview with NBC’s Meet the Press , Zelenskyy said American intelligence support had been temporarily blocked before being restored. The Ukrainian president expressed appreciation for the renewed cooperation, saying the arrangement was functioning again. According to Reuters , the intelligence is particularly important for Ukraine’s ability to detect Russian ballistic missile launches and prepare its air defenses. The restoration follows several days of uncertainty over Washington’s support for Ukraine amid disagreements between the administration of US President Donald Trump and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes against Russian energy infrastructure. Zelenskyy Says Ukraine Lost Missile Warnings for Three Days Zelenskyy said the interruption lasted three days, during which Ukraine did not receive critical American intelligence concerning Russian ballistic missile attacks. In remarks reported by European Pravda , the Ukrainian president explained that although dozens of countries provide Ukraine with intelligence assistance, the United States has unique capabilities for identifying Russian ballistic missile launches. The information allows Ukrainian forces to anticipate incoming attacks and helps air-defense systems prepare to intercept missiles before they reach their targets. Ukraine has faced repeated Russian strikes against cities, power facilities and other infrastructure, making advance warning an essential part of its national defense. Ballistic missiles are particularly challenging because they travel at extremely high speeds, reducing the time available for detection, warnings and interception. The reported interruption therefore raised concerns about gaps in Ukraine’s ability to respond to some of Russia’s most dangerous weapons. Trump Previously Denied Intelligence Cooperation Had Stopped The Ukrainian president’s latest comments contrast with earlier statements from Trump, who maintained that Washington was continuing to provide intelligence assistance to Kyiv. On October 14, Zelenskyy said the Trump administration had warned Ukraine that intelligence sharing could be suspended unless Ukrainian forces stopped attacking Russian oil refineries. Ukraine has defended its strikes on Russian energy facilities, arguing that such operations weaken Moscow’s capacity to finance and sustain its military campaign. Washington, however, has expressed concerns about attacks affecting global energy supplies and diplomatic efforts to negotiate an end to the war. The Kyiv Independent reported that Zelenskyy confirmed the intelligence interruption during Sunday’s interview, while Trump had previously insisted that cooperation was continuing. The precise operational scope of the suspension remains unclear. No detailed public explanation from Washington has independently established which intelligence services were affected or why the interruption occurred. US-Ukraine Relations Face Renewed Diplomatic Pressure The development comes amid growing tensions between Kyiv and Washington over sanctions against Russia, energy policy and military assistance. Trump has criticized Ukraine’s attacks against Russian oil infrastructure, while Zelenskyy has maintained that Ukraine must retain the ability to strike facilities that support Moscow’s war effort. The disagreement intensified as Russian attacks continued against Ukrainian energy infrastructure, placing additional pressure on Kyiv’s defenses. A separate Reuters report published on October 17 examined the growing differences between Trump and Zelenskyy, including disputes over economic sanctions, Russian oil exports and American security assistance. Despite those disagreements, Ukraine continues to seek cooperation with Washington on military support and diplomatic initiatives aimed at ending the war. Zelenskyy indicated that further discussions with American officials could take place during the coming week. On Sunday, he also disclosed contacts with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner concerning diplomatic efforts and possible next steps. The restoration of intelligence sharing addresses an immediate concern for Ukraine’s air defenses, although broader disagreements between Washington and Kyiv remain unresolved. For Ukraine, continued access to American missile-warning intelligence remains particularly important as Russian air attacks continue and diplomatic negotiations face uncertainty. ethiopia.content: The El-Alamein Quadrilateral and the Risks of Geopolitical Polarization in the North East Africa – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-10-21 The El-Alamein Quadrilateral and the Risks of Geopolitical Polarization in the North East Africa 0 Comments The rapid changes that are taking place in the North East Africa region shake the very foundation of the post-1991 geopolitical arrangement imposed on the Horn of Africa, Nile Basin and Red Sea. Ethiopia’s civilizational, cultural and national resilience is reshaping the regional geo-economic map linking the Nile Basin, Horn of Africa and Red Sea into one strategic theater. The operationalization of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam Nile (GERD) rewrites the geopolitical mathematics of the Nile with reason and fairness. Ethiopia’s emergence as a geo-economic game-changer in the geo-economically dormant terrain of the region activates the countries to utilize the waters of the Nile for their prosperity. South Sudan seeing this trend is intending to construct the Fula Dam to power its economy and safeguard its water security. Ethiopia, questioning the legitimacy of past decisions that deprived her of access to the sea, facing chokepoint wars, and anticipating maritime blockades, goes on striving for a durable access to the sea through a reasonable and fair manner. The new breed of leadership seeks to peacefully and legally redress the 1991 injustice that makes Ethiopia landlocked. This illegitimate act was undertaken by the late Egyptian Secretary-General of the UN Boutros Boutros-Ghali in league with the TPLF-Ethiopia and PFDJ-Eritrea. The strategic sea changes in the region re-graphing the “geo” of the Nile and Red Sea disputes Egypt’s regional vision built on absolute security architecture. The fundamental change in the basic structures of the regional system has forced Egyptian officials to stop the geopolitical rebalancing of the Horn. Egypt’s Foreign Minister authoring a commentary on News24 in 2025 underlined that Egypt is using its defense and diplomatic machinery to restore its dominium on the “two of the most important axes of Egyptian national security”—Nile Basin and Red Sea. Egypt’s militaristic and diplomatic posture took shape in October 2026 in El-Alamein, forming a Quadrilateral Security Grouping that includes PFDJ-Eritrea, SAF-Sudan and Hassan Sheikh-Somalia. The grouping seeks to re-configure the complicated waters of the Nile and Red Sea without Ethiopia. Egypt which is the brain behind this unilateral governance enterprise chariots the grouping to run the sovereignty of PFDJ-Eritrea, SAF-Sudan and Hassan Sheik-Somalia through Cairo. For Ethiopia, the significance of this assemblage lies not simply in the number of participating states, but in the implications of their emerging military and intelligence coordination for the region’s wider security architecture. The grouping defines Ethiopia as a structural challenger to the alliance and Egypt’s primacy in the region. The emerging security alliance advances Egypt’s Ethiopia strategy which is designed to exploit internal political differences through exporting instabilities. PFJD-Eritrea serves as a liaison in this project. The grouping seeks to promote the dismemberment scenario gaining meaning in the form of Tsimido materially steered by Egypt and PFDJ-Eritrea. This scenario seeking to embroil Ethiopia in “forever wars” intends to control the headwaters of Abay (Blue Nile) and decouple Addis Ababa from the Red Sea. This scenario is being countered by Ethiopia. Ethiopia’s military success, confusing the El-Alamein grouping and surprising the international commentariat, shows Ethiopia cannot be treated as a challenge to be contained but as a concrete pillar of the regional order built on indivisible security paired with open economic architecture. Besides the continued military and intelligence support, the El-Alamein grouping now turns to a full-fledged ideational war against Ethiopia in the global battle for hearts and minds. Egypt and PFJD-Eritrea are now engaged in diplomatic overdrive hell-bent on delegitimizing Ethiopia’s credibility and producing misinformation that materially disadvantage Ethiopia. The regime in Asmara depicts Ethiopia’s measured self-defense as an attempt to control PFDJ-Eritrea’s ports, turn Asmara into an Ethiopian coastal state, and make Addis Ababa a rule maker in the management of the Red Sea. Ethiopia’s peaceful search for sea access is sold by PFDJ-Eritrea and Egypt to the global audience as expansionism, controlling ports and revising the borders of the Horn. This is a scheme to cover up Eritrean incursion and El-Alamein grouping’s support to insurgent groups in Ethiopia. Besides delegitimizing Ethiopia’s reputation, this diplomatic smear campaign organized and directed by El-Alamein bloc is intended to contain Ethiopia as a “landlocked, truncated, weak and circumscribed country.” The El Alamein bloc entails that Egypt seeks to build its Red Sea position on keeping littoral states and non-littoral states apart in order to remake the geography and governance of the Red Sea without Ethiopia. For this to happen, Egypt does so by employing a combination of foreign-policy perceptions, economic pull, security coordination, and military support in the region. The framing of Red Sea for Red Sea littoral states advances closed regionalism and governance unilateralism, embracing Egypt’s conception of Arab Lake. The littoral-centric framing, originated with the formation of the Red Sea Council in 2020, evidently demonstrates the El-Alamein grouping’s policy to exclusively dictate the terms and rules of engagement on all issues of the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. This exclusively competitive approach risks producing overlapping security initiatives, diplomatic polarization and uncertainty for trade and investment in the broader region. The ultimate strategic goal of the El-Alamein grouping is all about undermining the peaceful restoration of Ethiopia’s legitimate access to its natural seashores by PFDJ/TPLF assisted by Egypt together with international complicity. That amounts to omitting Ethiopia’s historicity and ontology on the Red Sea. Professor Tecola Hagos captures this grim reality facing the Horn: “With Ethiopia landlocked, the long-term strategy for the Horn is terribly flawed.” With Ethiopia delinked from the Red Sea and barred from the governance of the water strip, the broader Red Sea and Gulf of Aden connected to the Middle East conflict has become a site of contest where land-based powers set to challenge the sea powers and an arena of zero-sum competition. The international community again sticks to the vocabulary and grammar of de-escalation regarding the tensions surrounding Ethiopia and PFDJ-Eritrea. PFDJ-Eritrea’s aversion to talking over fighting which seeks to profit from a contained, landlocked Ethiopia continues to bring insecurity and underdevelopment. Sadly, that war-footing behavior of PFDJ-Eritrea has brought, according to Hassan Umer Abdalla, “a sort of unconsumed divorce and impossible neighborliness” between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Partners with influence should not lose sight of the Eritrean problem fueled by Egypt’s hegemonic ambitions and turbocharged by rival regional security groupings, including, El-Alamein Quadrilateral Security bloc, that intend to corner and stop Ethiopia from ascending. The El-Alamein security arrangement cannot contribute to stability in the region as it is non-transparent, exclusive and negatively directed towards containing Ethiopia’s development. It has already become a source of mistrust Ethiopia perceives it as an instrument for constraining its legitimate national interests. The international partners plunging themselves in the content while leaving the terms of the conversation that trouble the Nile, Horn and Red Sea overlook the regional security logic—logic of dismemberment. The main objective of regional security architecture underpinned by this logic minted by Egypt is all about safeguarding the singular water, maritime and strategic interests against an existential threat from Ethiopia. Although Ethiopia as a resilient civilizational state has turned this logic of dismemberment into a myth, the same logic poses dangers to the security of the Nile and Horn while fueling the already contested wider Red Sea. The moment demands that the Horn of Africa finally break with the regressive regional architecture of “rules by few” and exclusion that continues to constrain and suffocate the future of the region with zero-sum rivalry and bloc politics. It demands that the Horn of Africa embrace tougher, harder, but more enabling paradigm of “rules through dialogue” and institutional inclusion replacing “rules by few” and unilateral governance. This enabling paradigm ensures that regional cooperation does not become a framework for strategic exclusion, opening new possibilities for the countries of the Horn to consult on and shape an open, inclusive regional architecture of mutual enablement that frames security as a shared responsibility and development as a shared empowerment. For this to happen, a new way of imagining agency, doing politics and exercising power is required by the region to deploy native intelligence and negotiate as a collective with the extended neighborhood—broader Arabian Peninsula—and the wider international community to seize the moment. As the global rules are being re-written in the fraying international order for survival and influence, will the Horn of Africa imagine, think and act otherwise to be an author of its future? ethiopia.title: Prisoner of History, Not Geography
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Prisoner of History, Not Geography - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Prisoner of History, Not Geography 20 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) opinion Addis Abeba — In early October 2026, Ethiopia and Eritrea took their quarrel to the UN Security Council by letter. Addis Abeba told council members that Eritrean troops had advanced up to 60 km into Tigray, which Eritrea denies. Asmara replied by calling the accusation a declaration of war and asking the council to take deterrent measures. Ethiopia also alleges that Eritrea is helping fund, mobilize, and direct armed groups in the north. Eritrea, for its part, says Addis Abeba is using its demand for sea access, along with the refrain that Ethiopia "cannot remain a prisoner of geography," as a pretext for military escalation. Officially, Ethiopia says it would pursue access through peace and dialogue. Beneath the exchange of letters lies a misunderstanding of geopolitical theory. When leaders frame Ethiopia, a country of more than 120 million people, as trapped in a landlocked cell by an accident of nature, they borrow shorthand from Tim Marshall's best-selling Prisoners of Geography . It is the kind of snappy line that makes a regional crisis sound like spatial fate. It is a compelling narrative, but it misreads physical geography. Ethiopia's landlocked condition is historical, legal, and political . That is not semantic pedantry; it dictates the cure. If a state is trapped by nature, only brute force or miraculous engineering can break its walls. If it is trapped by human choices, then diplomacy, international law, and regional trade corridors are the proper keys. What a "Prisoner of Geography" actually means Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Marshall's framework applies to immutable physical constraints: terrain that cannot be flattened, climates that cannot be negotiated with, and distances that cannot be erased. Russia is the classic case. Russia's western frontier rests on the North European Plain, a vast flat corridor from Germany to Moscow with no mountain range to stop an invader. Napoleon crossed it in 1812; Hitler in 1941. That vulnerability has driven centuries of Russian effort to push buffer zones westward. On the water, Russia has thousands of miles of coastline but few useful outlets. Murmansk stays ice-free but is hemmed in by the Greenland-Iceland-UK gap. The Black Sea fleet must pass through the Turkish-controlled Bosporus. The Baltic exits squeeze through the Danish straits, and Vladivostok is ice-affected in winter and tucked behind the Japanese archipelago. Catherine the Great's drive to the Black Sea answered this problem, and the problem has outlived her. Whether ruled by a Tsar, a Soviet commissar, or a modern president, the Kremlin keeps getting handed the same geography exam, and the water questions never get easier. This gives us a diagnostic test: a true prisoner of geography remains imprisoned no matter how many times the regime changes, the ideology shifts, or treaties are signed. Consider the rivers of Sub-Saharan Africa. The Congo and the Zambezi carry immense volumes of water, yet rapids, cataracts, and steep escarpments break them into disconnected stretches, preventing continuous navigation from the interior to the sea. Europe's navigable rivers carried goods straight to its ports. No act of parliament or diplomatic summit can persuade a waterfall to flow upstream. Applying the test to Ethiopia Ethiopia fails the test. Its topography is formidable: a volcanic highland massif carved by gorges and split by the Great Rift Valley, which made internal transport a historical challenge. But access to the Red Sea is a different spatial question. The coast is not separated from the highlands by impassable barriers, and Ethiopia has used it. Ethiopia's access to the sea has always been a matter of arrangements, not terrain. It reached the water first by the Franco-Ethiopian railway to Djibouti, which arrived in Addis Abeba in 1917, then, after the 1952 federation with Eritrea, through Assab and Massawa. Even after independence in 1993, cargo kept moving through Assab until the 1998-2000 war closed it. The land never changed. The paperwork did. Ethiopia's access to the sea has always been a matter of arrangements, not terrain." Ethiopia did not lose its coast because tectonic plates threw a tantrum or a mountain range erupted overnight. It lost the sea because of politics , the one force that can relocate a border faster than continental drift. The chain of events is long: Ottoman and Egyptian expansion along the coast; Italian colonization and the creation of Eritrea as a distinct unit; the 1952 UN federation ; the 1962 annexation under Emperor Haile Selassie; a thirty-year war of independence; the 1993 referendum ; and the breakdown of relations in 1998. Every link was a human decision. When Eritrea became independent, Assab became a foreign port, not because the earth shifted but because of a referendum that Ethiopia's own transitional government agreed to and the international community recognized. Ethiopia is not a prisoner of geography. It is a prisoner of history. Global Lessons: Bolivia, Switzerland, and international law The distinction between historical contingency and geographic destiny is well illustrated elsewhere. Bolivia lost its Pacific coastline to Chile in the War of the Pacific in the 1880s. Like Ethiopia, it became landlocked through a lost war and later treaties, not because a mountain range rose between its cities and the sea. Bolivia still marks a Day of the Sea each year and keeps a navy on Lake Titicaca, a remarkable act of national memory. Yet when it took Chile to the International Court of Justice , the court ruled in 2018 that Chile had no obligation to negotiate sovereign access. Bolivia's practical economic life has gone on through transit corridors and port facilities on the Chilean and Peruvian coasts. Switzerland, an Alpine nation with no coast, moves its exports down the Rhine to Rotterdam under negotiated transit arrangements with its neighbors. The pattern is clear: where landlocked status is the product of history and borders, commercial access is solved through law, diplomacy, and shared infrastructure, not by claiming a neighbor's territory. International law reflects this. Article 125 of the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea guarantees landlocked states a right of access to and from the sea and freedom of transit. It grants a right of transit, not a right to a sovereign coastline. The danger of misdiagnosis Misdiagnosing a political problem as geographic destiny is a dangerous policy mistake. If a nation convinces itself that it sits in a permanent cage imposed by nature, peaceful tools start to look inadequate, and force starts to look like liberation. To be fair to Addis Abeba, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed describes the quest for sea access as irreversible while stressing his commitment to diplomacy. But rhetoric about spatial entitlement has a way of outrunning the diplomacy it promises. The 1998-2000 war killed tens of thousands, devastated both economies, and ended with Ethiopia cut off from Assab, the opposite of its intended effect. Critics will say that Eritrea's own secession shows borders do change. They do, and the difference is consent. Eritrea's independence came through a referendum that Ethiopia's government accepted. Taking a port by force would set a different precedent: that population size or historical grievance justifies redrawing sovereign boundaries. On a continent whose borders were largely drawn by colonial cartographers, that principle would threaten the foundations of the African Union and, in time, Ethiopia's own boundaries. The alternatives are practical, if imperfect. Djibouti handles most of Ethiopia's trade, and diversifying through Berbera, Lamu, and Port Sudan would reduce dependence on it. Each comes with caveats: Berbera lies in Somaliland, whose status Somalia contests, and Port Sudan sits in a country at war. The strongest option is a negotiated commercial arrangement with Eritrea itself, such as port-use rights, shared infrastructure, and trade guarantees, built on the Algiers Agreement framework that both sides signed in 2000. Over-reliance on one corridor through Djibouti burdens Ethiopian businesses, creates strategic vulnerability and constrains a giant economy. Acknowledging that does not require mislabeling its cause. Russia cannot negotiate away the flat open corridor of the North European Plain, and African inland states cannot treaty away river cataracts. Ethiopia can negotiate, build, and trade its way to secure, diversified sea access. Geology may even help eventually: the Afar rift is slowly pulling Africa apart, and some geologists expect a new sea to form there in millions of years. Diplomacy is faster. Ethiopia is not locked in a natural prison. The cell was built by human history, and its door can be opened by human diplomacy. Conclusion The "prisoner of geography" narrative inherently invites military solutions, tempting leaders to enforce their will through force rather than diplomacy. Yet, territory and seaports seized at the barrel of a gun cannot deliver long-term security. True statesmanship lies in converting battlefield leverage into lasting political settlements before war becomes inevitable. Negotiation must not be a desperate last resort pursued only when ammunition is spent, and the economy has collapsed--as the Derg regime learned far too late after squandering its golden opportunities for peace. Real military maturity is measured by using power to forge peace while strong. As Scripture reminds us to remember our Creator in our youth, the optimal time to secure the Horn of Africa's future is during moments of strength. ethiopia.title: News - 13-Year-Old Girl Killed After Flag Dispute in Borana's Moyale - Protesters Block Transport Services
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: News - 13-Year-Old Girl Killed After Flag Dispute in Borana's Moyale - Protesters Block Transport Services - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: News - 13-Year-Old Girl Killed After Flag Dispute in Borana's Moyale - Protesters Block Transport Services 20 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — The opening of a new Somali Region administration office and the raising of its flag in Moyale town in Borana zone of Oromia regional state on October 18 triggered an exchange of gunfire between Somali regional forces and Oromia local militias, leaving a 13-year-old girl dead and prompting protests that disrupted transport services and forced businesses to close on Monday, residents told Addis Standard . Residents who spoke to Addis Standard accuse the Somali Region Police of shooting at the child and killing her instantly. Meanwhile, residents from the Somali side told Addis Standard that the girl was killed in crossfire between the two sides. Following the incident, elders and security officials reportedly agreed on Monday to remove the Somali Region's flag. However, the decision prompted demonstrations by Somali resident particularly in Kebele 02 on Tuesday that disrupted transport services and forced businesses and bus stations to close amid security fears. Mallicha Diida, a resident of Moyale's Kebele 02, told Addis Standard that the latest incident was part of a recurring cycle of violence in the town. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn "In Moyale, human blood has been spilled year after year. Last Sunday, when Somali Regional administration bodies opened a new mayor's office around Kebele 02 and hoisted the Somali Region flag, this act deeply angered many people," he said. Mallicha said gunfire subsequently broke out between Oromia militia members and Somali Region police, prompting the immediate intervention of the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF), which stopped the exchange. He alleged that Somali Region police shot and killed the 13-year-old girl, describing the incident as an act of "cruelty and lawlessness". He said the officers had killed the child rather than hold those responsible for any alleged wrongdoing accountable, claiming they accused her of throwing stones at them. A resident on the Somali side offered a different account, telling Addis Standard that the Somali-side Moyale town administration had merely relocated its office from its previous premises to a new location. "When they attempted to bring office equipment and hoist the flag, Oromia Region militias opened fire on the Somali Region police to prevent them from succeeding. The young girl was killed in the middle of this, but Somali Region security forces did not target or kill that child," the resident said, rejecting allegations that Somali Region forces were responsible for her death. All nine cases belong to a single cluster linked to the first patient, a Kenyan national who travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda and died in Nairobi on October 5. According to the Ministry’s press release signed by Director General Dr. Patrick Amoth, all eight surviving patients are “improving and responding well to treatment” and are currently stable. Kenya has received 500 doses of medicines to support treatment, and 134 of 135 contacts (99.3 percent) have been traced and quarantined, well above the global benchmark of 85 percent. The Ministry also announced that contacts who entered quarantine on October 6 will complete their 21-day monitoring period and begin returning home from Saturday, October 25. “Having completed 21 days without symptoms, they pose no risk of infection to anyone,” the statement said. What Kenya’s Success Means for Somalia On its face, Kenya’s containment of the cluster is good news for Somalia. A uncontrolled outbreak in Nairobi, Somalia’s primary transit hub for international travel and humanitarian logistics, would have immediate and severe consequences for Mogadishu. The fact that all nine cases remain linked to a single chain, with no evidence of community transmission, suggests that Kenya’s contact tracing and quarantine measures have functioned as intended. But Kenya’s success also sharpens the contrast with Somalia’s own preparedness. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the earlier phase of the outbreak , Somalia’s Cabinet approved a national Ebola preparedness committee in early October, and health authorities deployed staff to Mogadishu airport to monitor arriving travelers. The government also quarantined ten citizens who returned from the DRC through Uganda, and a Somali citizen who had travelled with the Kenyan victim was placed in isolation at Forlanini Hospital in Mogadishu. The critical weakness remains at the points of entry. A 2024 baseline assessment conducted with WHO Somalia found that Somalia’s International Health Regulations core capacities at points of entry averaged 27 percent, with airports at only 20 percent. The assessment noted no dedicated isolation areas, no biosecure transport for suspected cases, and no standard operating procedures for disease detection at Somali airports. The Kenyan index patient transited through Uganda and flew to Nairobi without being detected at the airport. If a similar case were to arrive in Mogadishu, Somalia’s screening infrastructure would face the same test. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the initial quarantine measures , the Somali citizen who travelled with the Kenyan victim passed through Mogadishu airport’s standard health screening without raising concerns. The Regional Picture Kenya’s nine cases are part of a broader regional emergency. The Bundibugyo strain outbreak in the DRC has now surpassed 9,500 confirmed cases and more than 4,600 deaths, making it the second deadliest Ebola outbreak on record. The strain has no approved vaccine or specific treatment, though trials are underway. Nigeria confirmed an imported case in October, and the WHO has warned that the geographic spread of the outbreak is the widest in history. Kenya’s Health Ministry has distributed supplies to 12 very high-risk and 16 high-risk counties, established a dedicated laboratory at Kenyatta National Hospital to handle Ebola testing without contaminating the main lab, and trained nearly 5,000 healthcare workers. The WHO has provided $70,000 in essential medical supplies, including PPE and testing kits. Somalia has received support from IGAD and WHO, including a joint mission that developed a costed Ebola preparedness and response workplan, and a national simulation exercise in September 2026 that tested detection, verification, and response protocols. The exercise identified gaps in reporting lines, notification and referral pathways, point-of-entry arrangements, and public communication. Critical Note Kenya’s handling of its first Ebola outbreak has been competent and transparent. The Ministry of Health has published regular updates, traced nearly all contacts, and kept the public informed without inducing panic. The decision to allow quarantined contacts to return home after 21 days is scientifically sound and socially responsible. But Somalia should not mistake Kenya’s success for its own safety. The same qualities that have allowed Kenya to contain its cluster, a functioning health ministry with laboratory capacity, trained personnel, and a coherent command structure, are precisely those that Somalia lacks. The Kenyan index patient flew from Uganda to Nairobi and was not detected at the airport. A similar case arriving in Mogadishu would encounter screening systems that a WHO assessment rated at 20 percent capacity, with no dedicated isolation areas and no biosecure transport. The window for Somalia to close these gaps is narrowing. Kenya’s cluster appears contained, but the DRC outbreak continues to accelerate, and the movement of people across East Africa is constant. The Somali government has established a preparedness committee and deployed staff to airports. Those are necessary first steps. They are not sufficient. The difference between Kenya and Somalia in this outbreak is not luck. It is institutional capacity. Until Somalia builds that capacity, its border defenses will remain a promise rather than a barrier. Share your story. Photo: Demetrius Freeman/The Washington Post via Getty Images The Trump administration is waging a multi-pronged war on Somali people, painting them as criminals, murderers, and terrorists and using multiple federal agencies to target them at home and abroad. The campaign includes military attacks in Somalia, as well as arrests, deportations, and the weaponization of federal law enforcement agencies against immigrants and the Somali American community in the United States, including the recent use of Homeland Security agents as a goon squad to target Minnesota congresswoman Ilhan Omar. In his second term, President Donald Trump has routinely cast Somalia as lawless and Somalis as violent . Meanwhile, his administration has, largely without public knowledge, killed hundreds of people in Somalia, claiming they belong to terror groups. Trump personally ordered the death of a Somali man within days of regaining the White House, according to his counterterrorism czar Sebastian Gorka. The administration claimed, without offering any evidence, that the man was connected with the Islamic State terror group. Trump has sought to do the same with Omar. Homeland Security agents raided Omar’s Washington, D.C., home last Monday, three weeks before the midterms , in which she is seeking reelection. The Trump administration reportedly launched the investigation to build a case to strip Omar of her U.S. citizenship and ultimately deport her. (Omar fled war in Somalia with her family when she was 8 years old, later immigrated to the U.S. as a refugee , and became a citizen in 2000.) The administration has also issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including to some of Omar’s relatives. On Monday, conservative media outlets reported that federal prosecutors obtained Omar’s DNA as part of their investigation. “This is what happens in a dictatorship. The leader identifies his political, ethnic and religious enemies, and his agents scramble to do his bidding and make him happy,” Zaynab Mohamed, a Somali immigrant who represents Minneapolis in Minnesota’s state Senate, told The Intercept. “Representative Omar is the latest subject where Trump identifies the target and his minions go looking for a crime. The cases always fall apart, and this one will, too.” Related DHS Was Designed as a Weapon Trump claimed not to have ordered the raid, but throughout his second term, his Justice Department has repeatedly targeted his political enemies — from New York’s attorney general , to the former head of the FBI, to members of the Federal Reserve. “I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ,” Trump said to reporters. “I have nothing to do with it.” Omar called it “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” She added: “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.” Omar’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment from The Intercept. With the Somali community , Trump found a target that he could attack with Islamophobic, racist, and xenophobic rhetoric , without incurring much mainstream backlash, said Jaylani Hussein, the executive director of the Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations. “As immigrants, Muslims, and — most importantly — Black people, it’s the trifecta,” he told The Intercept. “None of us expected the scale and level of the vitriol. But despite this, it’s at the point that the traditional media almost ignore the attacks on the Somali-American community because it’s not a large constituency. Trump says these things, and people just move on.” Most Read Inside ICE, Officials Question String of Trump Admin “Midterm Panic Moves” Karl Loftus Lockheed Martin Showered Susan Collins With Cash as F-35 Program Hit Turbulence Noah Hurowitz President Apocalypse Tom Engelhardt Trump’s War on Somalia Over the last decade, Trump has overseen the killing of as many as 1,500 Somalis in more than 400 attacks, according to a count by New America, a D.C.-based think tank. During his second term alone, the Trump administration has conducted more than 200 airstrikes in Somalia, including close to 90 this year, claiming to target terrorists. The U.S. military has been at war in Somalia for almost a quarter-century, conducting air attacks and commando raids aimed at the terrorist group al-Shabab as well as the Islamic State group, while the CIA and special operators created local proxy forces to conduct low-profile operations on behalf of America. At the same time, the U.S. has provided Somalia with billions of dollars in counterterrorism assistance. Related U.S. Conducts “Largest Airstrike in the History of the World” (Sort Of) U.S. attacks in Somalia have skyrocketed during Trump’s terms in office. From 2007 to 2017, under the administrations of George W. Bush and Barack Obama, the U.S. military carried out 59 declared airstrikes in Somalia. The Biden administration conducted 51 declared strikes over four years. During Trump’s six years in office, the U.S. has launched more than 400 attacks against purported militants. The U.S. rarely offers any evidence that those killed are members of terrorist groups, much less leaders. A New America analysis found militant leaders comprised just 1.7 percent of those killed. Africa Command refused to provide requested evidence that any of those killed in airstrikes in Somalia this year were militants. “All U.S. strikes in Somalia are conducted in close coordination partners [sic] against designated terror groups,” an AFRICOM spokesperson told The Intercept by email. “Trump has conducted more drone strikes in Somalia than Bush, Obama, and Biden combined. And so many civilians have died,” historian Elizabeth Schmidt, the author of “Foreign Intervention in Africa After the Cold War: Sovereignty, Responsibility, and the War on Terror,” told The Intercept. “They were often just young men living in an area where it was easy to label them jihadis. And it turns out they had nothing to do with terrorism.” The U.S. claims that it has only killed six civilians over almost two decades of war in Somalia. A count by the airstrike monitoring group Airwars put the number at as much as 2,600 percent higher . A 2023 investigation by The Intercept determined, for example, that a drone attack in Somalia during Trump’s first term killed at least three, and possibly five, civilians, including 22-year-old Luul Dahir Mohamed and her 4-year-old daughter Mariam Shilow Muse. At the time of the attack, the U.S. announced it had killed “ five terrorists ” and that “no civilians were killed in this airstrike.” Trump calls Somalia a “third-world” or “ fourth-world nation ,” says that it “ stinks ,” and disparaged Somalis who come to the U.S., saying “we’re going to go the wrong way if we keep taking in garbage into our country.” His most xenophobic consigliere also claims Somalia is responsible for violence that has caused people to flee the country. “The entire Somali refugee program is predicated on a lie,” wrote Trump’s deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, Stephen Miller, late last year. “Destroying your own country does not give you the right to become a citizen in ours.” But this faux history disregards America’s decadeslong role in fomenting violence in Somalia and destabilizing the country. “The presence of Somalis in the U.S. has a lot to do with U.S. wars in Somalia.” A casualty of the Cold War geopolitics that led to widespread conflict, political repression, and millions of deaths across the developing world, Somalia has experienced persistent political instability and strife since the late 1960s. In recent decades, the country has suffered civil war, famine, droughts, a longtime al-Shabab insurgency, and persistent humanitarian crises. Related Who Could Have Predicted the U.S. War in Somalia Would Fail? The Pentagon. Over the last quarter century, the U.S. has intensified conflict in Somalia through direct attacks; training, funding, and running proxy forces; and funneling in weapons and other military assistance to one side of a civil war. As early as 2007, the Pentagon was aware that there were fundamental flaws with U.S. military operations in the Horn of Africa, and Somalia devolved into another forever war stalemate. This has continued, despite the record number of airstrikes in Somalia under Trump. Before Trump took office, in 2016, Islamist militants in Somalia killed 4,281 people , according to the Africa Center for Strategic Studies, a Pentagon research institution. By August, this year’s total hit 6,731 deaths, a 57 percent increase. An analysis by the Costs of War project at Brown University found that instead of eliminating militant groups, the U.S. counterterrorism campaign in Somalia was “ensuring that the conflict continues in perpetuity.” An AFRICOM spokesperson said the command’s “operational focus remains on working with partners to degrade terrorist organizations to create the space required for Somali-led governance and stability.” But Trump claims Somalia has no government , no military , and is “ not even a country .” “ They weren’t coming because they wanted a better job. It’s because they feared for their lives and their children’s lives.” The Intercept interviewed people displaced by the forever war in a camp on the outskirts of Somalia’s capital, Mogadishu, in 2023. “We had to leave because of the drought and the conflict,” a mother of seven told this reporter. She was one of more than a dozen women from the Lower Shabelle region of southwest Somalia who spoke to The Intercept after fleeing the front lines of an offensive by the U.S.-backed Somali government against al-Shabab. Since Trump first took office, the number of Somalis forced from their homes has almost doubled from 2.4 million to 4.4 million. “I don’t think most Americans realize that the presence of Somalis in the U.S. has a lot to do with U.S. wars in Somalia. U.S. military intervention made a bad situation worse. This led to a surge of refugees and asylum-seekers to the U.S.,” said Schmidt. “They weren’t coming because they wanted a better job. It’s because they feared for their lives and their children’s lives.” During Trump’s first term, his administration acknowledged “ the ongoing armed conflict ” as a reason to extend temporary protected status — which grants legal status, work authorization, and protection from deportation — to Somalis in the U.S., noting the security situation was “fragile and volatile, with ongoing armed conflict among government forces, clan militias, African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) troops, and al-Shabaab.” We’re independent of corporate interests — and powered by members. More than 1,000 Somali asylum-seekers have been ordered deported since February; more than half the deportation orders involve Somalis living in Minnesota, a nearly tenfold increase from 2025, according to a Minnesota Star Tribune investigation. About 84,000 of the 260,000 people of Somali descent in the U.S. live in the Minneapolis–St. Paul area, according to the Census Bureau’s annual American Community Survey. The overwhelming majority are American citizens. Almost 58 percent were born in the U.S. and 87 percent of foreign-born Somalis are naturalized citizens. Related Unnamed Source in Viral Minnesota Somali Fraud Video Is Right-Wing Lobbyist Who Called Muslims “Demons” The administration targeted that Somali community during a violent immigration crackdown in and around Minneapolis known as “ Operation Metro Surge ” during late 2025 and early 2026. “I don’t want them in our country,” Trump said in December 2025. The next month, he said: “Every one of them should be forced to leave this country, including Ilhan Omar.” During Metro Surge, federal agents shot and killed protesters Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti . They, like Omar and hundreds of drone strike victims in Somalia, were labeled as terrorists by the administration without providing evidence. “If the president can threaten to denaturalize and deport a member of Congress, no one is safe.” During Trump’s second term, Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have also arrested hundreds of Somali people, with reports of assault and mistreatment at the hands of federal agents. Trump recently seemed to call for vigilante violence and threatened to back it with federal force. “The once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants,” Trump posted on Truth Social earlier this month. “The Somalians should not be allowed to get away with what they are doing. They view you as weak and stupid people. Fight back Minnesota, fight back! If you need, the Federal Government will come to your rescue.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment. Hussein, of CAIR-MN, said Trump’s rhetoric was endangering the Somali community. “Every few weeks, he’s literally going on a tirade. And I don’t think he’s ever spoken about other people the same way. He literally put out the message saying, ‘go fight them. I’ll come and help’ on social media,” he told The Intercept. “We’ve seen bullying. We’ve dealt with harassment. We’ve have some assaults.” Related Trump Is Targeting Ilhan Omar. Where’s the Elite Media Outrage? Trump has routinely demonized Somalis by tying the broader community to a high-profile fraud case : the alleged theft of $250 million from a pandemic-era program that provided food for children. The former leader of Feeding Our Future, the nonprofit at the center of the case, is white, although most of the defendants in the related cases are of Somali descent. “The Somalians, they’re crooked as hell,” Trump ranted at a Cabinet meeting in May, with the administration offering escalating and unverified claims, including reference to a “ $19 billion Somali fraud scandal .” The Trump administration’s effort to denaturalize and deport Omar is part of a broader push to strip naturalized Americans of their citizenship, with those of Somali descent specifically singled out. “I would do it in a heartbeat if they were dishonest,” Trump said in an Oval Office interview earlier this year. “I think that many of the people that came in from Somalia, they hate our country.” Trump’s border czar Tom Homan said on Saturday that he had been “told they have a strong case” against Omar. “Of course, if you lie during the naturalization process, there is a process to denaturalize somebody. We’ve done it before,” he told Fox News. The rarely used denaturalization statute has been most famously employed to strip citizenship from Nazi war criminals , like John Demjanjuk, a former death camp guard and retired U.S. autoworker convicted on 28,060 counts of being an accessory to murder. Mohamed, who in 2022 became the first Somali woman elected to the Minnesota Senate, called out Trump’s push to expel Omar as a grave threat to the country. “If the president can threaten to denaturalize and deport a member of Congress, no one is safe,” she told The Intercept. “This is a test of our democracy, and even Republicans should be speaking out about it. If we don’t defend the rights of Ilhan Omar, Somali-Americans, immigrants, and Trump’s political targets, we lose everything.” Share Copy link Share on Facebook Share on Bluesky Share on X Share on LinkedIn Share on WhatsApp IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. The agreement, signed on October 13 in Athens during the Rethinking Governance for a Changing World conference, aims to strengthen institutional cooperation between Morocco's École Nationale de l'Administration (ENA) and Somalia's National University (SNU). The MoU focuses on exchanging expertise and best practices in public administration, leadership, and management competency development. This initiative is part of broader efforts to improve governance and administrative reform in both countries, ultimately enhancing the efficiency and responsiveness of public institutions to citizens' needs.

somalia.content: Hormuud Telecom hosts fifth Somali Success Story Forum focused on healthcare sector Latest Headlines Hormuud Telecom hosts fifth Somali Success Story Forum focused on healthcare sector Tigray rebels claim to have killed over 1,500 Ethiopian soldiers as PM Abiy Ahmed warns Eritrea Somalia: Puntland Health Minister Inspects Dhahar Hospital During Regional Tour Christiane Amanpour to Leave CNN in 2027 After 43 Years Somalia’s Opposition Alliance to Hold Key Political Talks in Nairobi, Kenya Advertise with us Home News Puntland Somalia World Sports Press Releases Somaliland Videos Opinion Contact Privacy Policy English Somali Hormuud Telecom hosts fifth Somali Success Story Forum focused on healthcare sector Omar Nor, Chief Editor GAROWE ONLINE Posted On 21-10-2026, 09:30AM MOGADISHU, Somalia — Somalia’s leading telecommunications company Hormuud Telecom on Tuesday hosted the fifth edition of the Somalia’s Success Story Forum (BGS26) in Mogadishu, bringing together around 350 participants to discuss investment in healthcare and ways to improve medical services in the country. Held at Jazeera Hotel under the theme “Towards a Healthy Somalia”, the forum focused on healthcare investment, expanding access to medical services and addressing gaps in infrastructure and service delivery. Somalia’s Health Minister, Dr Ali Haji Adam, who officially opened the event, said investment in healthcare was essential to building a healthy society and a developed nation. He welcomed the focus on health, saying the country needed to recognise progress, confront persistent challenges and work collectively towards better medical services. "Investing in healthcare is not merely a financial commitment, but an investment in building a healthy society and a developed nation," said Dr. Ali Haji Adan, Somalia's Minister of Health, commending the convening of the forum. In his keynote speech, Hormuud Telecom Chairman Ahmed Mohamed Yusuf said healthcare was chosen as this year’s forum theme because of its importance to Somali society. He praised health workers’ efforts and said the forum aimed to recognise their contributions, strengthen public confidence in local healthcare and encourage hospitals to expand specialised services. “We chose to focus on healthcare in Somalia this year because of its vital importance to people’s lives. We commend Somalia’s healthcare professionals for their dedication and the progress they have made in advancing the country’s health sector. We organised this forum to recognise their contributions, encourage their continued efforts, and strengthen public confidence in our country’s healthcare services,” Yusuf said. The Minister of Planning, Investment and Economic Development, Hon. Mohamud Abdirahman Benabene, commended Somalia’s Success Story Forum (BGS26), highlighting its importance to the Somali people and Hormuud Telecom’s role in organising the forum. The Minister also emphasised the importance of healthcare in advancing social development and building a healthy nation. Communications and Technology Minister Mohamed Aden Moallim Ali said technology and innovation could improve access to healthcare and support the development of a modern, sustainable health system. Senator Dufle called for a unified organisation representing Somali doctors to help coordinate and improve medical services nationwide. He also conveyed congratulations from Senate Speaker Abdi Hashi Abdullahi to Somalia’s Success Story Forum (BGS26). Somalia’s first Cancer specialist Hussein Hassan Abshir addressed the burden of cancer in Somalia. He claimed that 80 percent of Somalis travelling to India for medical treatment were found to have cancer at an advanced stage when treatment was no longer possible. The figure was not independently verified. Yasin Mohamud Ibar, chairman of the Somali Chamber of Commerce and Industry, called for stronger cooperation between the government and private sector, saying partnerships could help deliver quality, affordable healthcare that people could access more easily. A key part of Somalia’s Success Story Forum (BGS26) was a panel discussion on building healthcare services that are affordable, accessible, and equitable and of high quality. The discussion examined in depth the challenges hindering improvements in Somalia’s healthcare services and explored potential solutions for the future. Deputy Prime Minister Jibril Abdirashid Haji formally closed the forum, praising its organisation and Hormuud Telecom’s role in supporting community initiatives and the development of essential services. Hormuud organises the annual Somalia’s Success Story Forum to promote innovation, investment and development by bringing together government officials, businesses, experts and development partners. This year’s event focused on strengthening Somalia’s healthcare system. The meeting focused on improving cooperation among government agencies, strengthening passenger safety, and advancing the clearance of designated facilities near the facility. The minister emphasized the need to expedite the evacuation plan for structures slated for relocation or demolition, describing Aden Adde as a vital entry point and an important symbol of Somalia’s international connectivity. The inspection was attended by the State Minister for Transport and Civil Aviation and other senior officials. A Pattern with Precedent The government’s push to clear structures around the airport is not new. The facility’s location within Mogadishu’s urban fabric has long presented security challenges, particularly given the persistent threat from Al-Shabaab , which has targeted the airport and the surrounding area with mortars in the past. What is notable about the current plan is its resonance with a broader, well-documented pattern of forced evictions and land seizures in Mogadishu. A Heritage Institute for Policy Studies report published in October 2026 found that between 2017 and September 2026, 2,136,420 people were evicted across Somalia, with 64 percent of those evictions occurring in the Benadir region, which encompasses the capital. The report documents a shift in the nature of evictions . In 2021, only 11 percent of evictions from Mogadishu’s displacement camps occurred on government-owned land. By 2025, that figure had risen to 44 percent. The state has transitioned from bystander to evictor, with demolitions often conducted without adequate notice, consultation, or compensation. In August 2026, violence erupted in Mogadishu’s Tookiyo neighbourhood when government forces clashed with residents protesting the demolition of their homes, leaving nearly 10 people injured, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the clashes . Similar confrontations occurred in Wabari, where government forces used live ammunition against residents resisting eviction, and in Daynile, where rival security factions clashed over demolitions in the Warlaliska neighbourhood. The Heritage Institute report attributes the crisis in part to a governance vacuum. The Benadir Regional Administration and the Ministry of Public Works dispute responsibility for urban land, creating what the report describes as an opening for “predatory political and commercial elites” to enrich themselves at the public’s expense. Developers use administrative decrees to acquire valuable land without competitive tendering or verification of ownership, and connected buyers rely on state security forces to evict occupants. The Union of Somali Islamic Scholars Councils intervened in August 2026, calling on the government to halt demolitions and investigate land seizures. The scholars said they had received complaints from residents who claimed to possess legal ownership documents but had their property challenged, seized, or subjected to fees with no clear legal basis, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the scholars’ intervention . What the Airport Plan Does Not Say Authorities have not disclosed the number of structures affected by the airport clearance plan, the specific neighbourhoods targeted, or the timeline for the proposed relocation and demolition exercise. The lack of detail leaves residents in the vicinity of the airport facing uncertainty about whether their homes or businesses will be affected, and what compensation or resettlement arrangements, if any, will be offered. Historical precedent offers little reassurance. In 2010, Somali security agents demolished approximately 500 homes near the airport, citing fears that they could be used as cover for insurgent attacks. Hundreds of families were left without shelter, and a BBC reporter at the time noted there was no evidence the government provided the land it had promised and Somali Political Elites ended up benefiting from the projects and building villas in the cleared area near the airport.. Critical Note The security rationale for clearing the airport buffer zone is genuine. Aden Adde serves as Somalia’s principal international gateway, and its proximity to densely populated areas increases the risk of collateral damage from any attack. A major security incident at the airport would be devastating for the government’s credibility and for the country’s connections to the outside world. But the government’s approach to land clearance in Mogadishu has a documented history that makes skepticism reasonable. The Heritage Institute’s findings, the pattern of violent confrontations in Tookiyo, Wabari, and Daynile, and the scholars’ intervention all point to the same conclusion: demolitions and evictions in the capital have too often served private interests rather than public ones. If the airport clearance follows the same pattern, it risks becoming another chapter in a land crisis that has already displaced more than two million people. The government has not yet published the details of this plan. Until it does, the residents of the airport zone have no way of knowing what will happen to them, and the public has no way of assessing whether the security benefits justify the human costs. The minister’s meeting produced a directive. It did not produce accountability, transparency, or a compensation framework. Those are the elements that would distinguish a legitimate security measure from another episode of state-enabled land capture. Share your story. somalia.content: Families fleeing Somalia crises find bleak prospects in Dadaab refugee camps - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Families fleeing Somalia crises find bleak prospects in Dadaab refugee camps Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Tuesday October 20, 2026 Nurto fled conflict in Baidoa and is struggling to support her seven children in Dadaab refugee camps/Ahmed Abdulahi/Ergo Families fleeing adversity in different parts of southern Somalia have been arriving in Kenya’s Dadaab refugee camps, where they find themselves with no means of making a living nor aid or support. They include families fleeing conflict in Baidoa, house demolitions by the Somali government in Mogadishu, and drought in their home areas. advertisements The new arrivals say they have received no reception support, shelter, or other forms of aid. Some are staying with relatives already struggling to make ends meet, while others have settled on their own on vacant land in Dadaab’s Ifo-2 camp. They lack food, housing, toilets and other basic services. Nurto Mohamed Ali, who arrived in Ifo-2 on 20 August, said her family had received no assistance and was struggling to meet basic needs. She is staying with relatives who arrived earlier. “Neighbours collect maize and cooking oil for us. That is how we are surviving now,” she said. “We have children who need food and bedding, but we have nothing to give them.” Nurto fled ongoing conflict in Baidoa between federal government forces and those loyal to the former South West State administration. She was a farmer raising her family on their two-hectare plot of land in Baidoa. Separated from her husband, she receives no support from him and is the sole income earner. In the refugee camp now, her seven children often go to bed hungry because she lacks food. They occupy a shelter made from plastic sheets, cloth and thorny branches in the yard of a relatives’ home – a household of 10. The days reach a scorching 37°C and the rainy season has begun. Nurto and her older children have to sleep outside without bedding while the youngest children cram themselves into the hut. Nurto said they had expected to receive assistance on arrival, including refugee registration cards, household items, and a house. She has received nothing. “We have no proper house, and even the people who arrived before us do not have one. The shelter situation is very difficult. We sleep on pieces of cloth and a small, broken mat,” she said. Other vulnerable new arrivals, including older people, people with disabilities, women and children, are finding no formal help in the camp, where some walk around daily asking more established residents for food. Hawo Mohamed Ali, her disabled husband, and their 10 children arrived in Ifo-2 on 1 August. They fled Mogadishu’s Hodan district after the government demolished their house, saying the land belonged to the state. They had lived in the house for 34 years without having formal land ownership documents. She said losing the home made it impossible for her family to remain in Mogadishu. “When we left and went outside, we found our land fenced off and surrounded by a wall,” she told Radio Ergo. “We were told the land would be measured and returned to us. Our houses were demolished using bulldozers, and we thought the land would be given back. Later, we were told it was government land and that we had to leave.” The demolition left Hawo’s family homeless and they decided their only option was to seek refuge in Dadaab. In Mogadishu, she earned a living selling meat and watermelon in local markets. In the refugee camp, however, they have not been registered and haven’t received aid cards or assistance. She looked for laundry work, but the jobs are irregular, so she has to ask others for help with food for her children. She lacks firewood and containers for collecting water. “The children’s father is disabled, and life is very difficult for us. My children are still young and have nothing here. We left our home and came to a place we do not know,” said Hawo, adding that the conditions in Dadaab were far worse than she had expected. The chairman of Hagardera camp, Khalif Dhubow Jelle, said the hardship facing new arrivals from Somalia had been brought to the attention of humanitarian agencies in the camps, but no effective response had followed. He recorded nearly 250 families having arrived from southern Somalia in the past three months. “Their living conditions are extremely poor. It is also the rainy season, yet these people have no shelter or place to stay. They are sitting in the open and have no food or water,” he said. The new arrivals are joining a refugee population already struggling with difficult living conditions because of reduced humanitarian aid and wider economic hardship across the camps. somalia.summary: Families fleeing crises in Somalia are facing dire conditions in the Dadaab refugee camps in Kenya. The camps, originally established to accommodate a temporary influx of refugees, are now home to over 200,000 people, leading to overcrowding and limited resources. Many refugees are struggling with inadequate access to food, clean water, and healthcare. The ongoing conflict, drought, and famine in Somalia have driven families to seek safety, but the camps offer little hope for a better future. Aid organizations are overwhelmed and unable to meet the growing needs of the population, leaving many refugees in a state of uncertainty and despair. The situation highlights the urgent need for international support and sustainable solutions to address the challenges faced by displaced families.
